newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's OECD entry to boost deregulation - analysts.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's OECD entry to boost deregulation - analysts.

text.p: South Korea's entry into the OECD club of rich nations would speed up the government's deregulation drive, analysts said on Saturday.
But critics and opposition parties warn against the adverse impact of further prying open local markets to offshore competition, especially on small and medium-sized industries.

Friday's decision by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) to invite South Korea into the Paris-based group of industrialised nations has met enthusiastic applause from finance ministry officials.
Seoul predicts the long-sought invitation will be swiftly ratified by South Korea's 299-seat National Assembly, in which President Kim Young-sam's ruling party has a slim majority.

"I see little problem at the parliament as opposition parties would not want to see the nation's image hurt by a rejection," Hyun Jung-taik, Director-General for the ministry's International Economic Policy Bureau, told Reuters.

The government's optimism appeared justified on Saturday after the main opposition party announced it would reconsider its stance on entry into the 28-member OECD, backing away from a vow on Friday to block the move in parliament.
"There has been no change in our stance that it's too early for the nation to join the club," said Chung Dong-young, a spokesman for the National Congress for New Politics party.
"But now that the decision was made, we see the necessity for reconsideration," he added.

Critics fear OECD membership will only hamper the economy by triggering a rush of foreign competition which could squeeze local small to medium sized firms while raising the risk of a volatile share market by attracting more offshore funds.

"Smaller firms have owed much of their business to various protective policies by the government. But now, the government would not be able to continue this," said Lee Hahn-ku, president of the Daewoo Research Institute.
The Citizens Coalition for Economic Justice, one of South Korea's major lobby groups, said it would mount nationwide campaign to block ratification of OECD admission.

"Entry at this time, when financial industries are not prepared for foreign competition, would only stir chaos," said Ra Young-sam, a senior official at the coalition. "It's absolutely premature and we will block it."
Since the early 1990s, South Korea has taken steps to slowly open its markets, offering to announce new measures to speed up the process if it won OECD membership.

On October 1, the ceiling on foreign ownership in local stocks was raised to 20 percent for most South Korean listed companies from 18 percent. The government has pledged to expand the ceiling by three percentage points every year by 1999.
Foreign investment in unsecured corporate bonds issued by small and medium-sized firms will be allowed from late 1998.

Analysts said the huge gap between South Korea's long-term interest rates, now hovering over 12 percent, and the lower rates of most OECD-member nations could attract a rush of speculative funds into South Korea.
"Whether we gain or lose from the admission will depend on how well the government can prepare for every possible scenario," said Lee of Daewoo.

An OECD statement on Friday said South Korea would be the 11th largest exporter in the OECD zone and accounted for about 2.5 percent of world exports, a position which had been enhanced through liberalisation of its own import controls.
South Korea would be the second Asian nation after Japan to become a member at the club. From the wider Asia-Pacific area, Australia and New Zealand are also members of the OECD.
